guideword: FORM/USE: 'NOT ONLY … BUT ALSO' WITH INVERSION
can_do_statement: Can use inverted auxiliary 'do' + the subject after 'not only', to give focus.
example_raw:
Indeed, not only did they teach us useful knowledge, but they also organised practical exercises to ensure that we had assimilated all the information. (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2006; Greek; Pass)

Furthermore, not only do I speak (and write) in fluent English, but I also speak French, Spanish and Portuguese. (Brazil; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2004; Mende; Pass)

For me, not only do extreme sports provide satisfaction of achievement, but they also help you to express yourself. (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2008; Greek; Pass)

positives: Indeed, not only did they teach us useful knowledge, but they also organised practical exercises.
Not only do I speak fluent English, but I also speak French.
negatives: He did not only do his homework, but he also washed the dishes.
Not only are they nice, they are also smart.

can_do_statement: Can use '(and) yet' to combine phrases and clauses to introduce a contrast, often unexpected.
example_raw:
In the face of these recent events, our department also reviewed the contract with ProLine International, and found some interesting yet unpleasant details. (Romania; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2007; Romanian; Fail)

This college is famous for its art teachers and very skilled students, and yet it does not have its own gallery. (C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2006; Polish; Pass)

The host family was carefully selected, yet it was four miles away from school. (Poland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1993; Polish; Pass)

positives: The host family was carefully selected, yet it was four miles away.
I saw it, and yet it felt weird.

can_do_statement: Can use 'And yet' to combine sentences to introduce a contrast, often unexpected, sometimes in a formal context.
example_raw:
If I had, I would try to do the best for them, just like my parents did, and very likely I would make the same mistakes. And yet, I think I would be a good and loving father. (Germany; C2 MASTERY; 1993; German; Pass)

I felt very embarrassed and I was sure I would get the sack. And yet the manager forgave me and I continued to work there. (Poland; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Polish; Pass)

positives: It was raining. And yet, we went out.
And yet the manager forgave me.
negatives: I haven't gone out and played yet.
The host family was carefully selected, yet it was four miles away.

can_do_statement: Can use 'not only … but also' to combine phrases and clauses, often for focus or emphasis.
example_raw:
This book is not only a guide to the history of music but also a compendium of theory. (Spain; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 1999; Catalan; Pass)

In addition to that, if we move to the new premises, we can not only solve the above problems, but also gain other benefits such as a better environment. (China; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2008; Chinese; Fail)

If we go back in time we will see that the difference between the old and the modern films is not only the number produced but also the content. (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2007; Greek; Pass)

positives: This book is not only a guide to the history of music but also a compendium of theory.
If we move we can not only solve the problems, but also gain other benefits.
negatives: Not only do I speak fluent English, but I also speak French.
Not only did they run, but they also hid.

can_do_statement: Can use 'because' as a subordinating conjunction to introduce a subordinate clause.
example_raw:
I want a big garden because I have children. (Arabic - Other)

She likes meeting other people because she wants to improve her English. (Nepali)

positives: I want a big garden because I have children.
She likes meeting other people because she wants to improve her English.
negatives: Because of the rain, we stayed inside.
I did it just because of you.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of simple subordinating conjunctions ('as, after, before since, until, although, whether, so (that), though') to introduce a subordinate clause.
example_raw:
In fact, I have to buy a desk, as I don't have one. (French)

I usually read during the afternoon after I have finished my homework. (Italian) 

Before going out in the centre, we went to a pub in order to eat something together, but I didn't see my boyfriend because he stayed at home. (Italian)

I haven't seen him since we were at school. (Portuguese)

I'm really sorry that I'm not available to attend this since I'll be in China for an important meeting with a customer. (Chinese)

But I didn't remember my ring until I got back home. (Korean)

Although the holiday was fantastic, I wished that you were with us. (Afrikaans)

My parents also want me to go on holiday with them this summer, although I want to stay with my friends. (German)

There were lots of people waiting for us though we had never met them before. (French)

You gave it to me so that I could fix it! (Bengal)

positives: I haven't seen him since we were at school.
But I didn't remember my ring until I got back home.

can_do_statement: Can use more complex subordinating conjunctions ('as long as, as soon as, in order that, despite the fact that, due to the fact that, as if, as though') to introduce a subordinate clause.
example_raw:
As far as I am concerned, keeping animals in zoos is not cruel as long as the zoos keep to certain rules concerning the conditions the animals have to be kept in. (Dutch)

I decided to go to Paris as soon as I finished university. (Spanish - Latin American)

The jazz, rock and classical concerts were really entertaining except that there were some concert halls which were too small for the audience. (Korean) 

So take a rest in your hotel, in order that you can be prepared for your packed schedule. (Greek)

To sum up, the festival was successful, so I hope most people enjoyed the festival despite the fact that there were some problems with the poor sound system, and so on. (Korean)

Due to the fact that the mass of cars pollute the cities and the environment, we are forced to give up our city habits and learn to be more sensible by using public transportation. (German)

From the window of my room I could see her every night, as if she was the great mother of the sky. (Portuguese)

Everything was so familiar, so close, as though he had never left the place. (Russia; B2 VANTAGE; 1997; Russian; Pass)

positives: I decided to go to Paris as soon as I finished university.
Everything was so familiar, as though he had never left the place.
negatives: I have as many as you.
It is due to the weather.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of simple subordinating conjunctions ('once, whereas, unless, except (that) provided (that)'), to introduce a subordinate clause.
example_raw:
Believe me, once you have tried it, you'll never give it up. (Spanish - Latin American)

Once you become an employee, you'll get discounts on books and CDs. (French)

Some of us find it very useful whereas others still have difficulty in accepting technology as a valuable thing for everyone. (Polish)

Getting to work by car is comfortable, and faster unless you are caught in a traffic jam. (Poland; B2 VANTAGE; 1993; Polish; Pass)

Unless the situation improves, we will be forced to try a new supplier. (Romanian)

Whenever I walk down the street, I always want to go into every shop. (Korean)

I can't say that I’ve changed much, except that now I'm blond! (Brazil; B2 VANTAGE; 2003; Portuguese; Pass)

It offers special services for students provided you show your student card. (Japanese)

Also, provided that some customers are always in the shops, the electricity is not really "wasted". (Japanese)

positives: Once you become an employee, you'll get discounts.
I can't say that I've changed much, except that now I'm blond!

can_do_statement: Can use a limited range of simple subordinating conjunctions '(if, when, so, while)' to introduce a subordinate clause.
example_raw:
But if you don't take your car, you can rent a bike in the park too. (French)

If I need a camera, I will use my mobile phone. (Turkish)

My father bought it for me when he saw my grades at school. (Greek)

When you buy a pair of shoes, the second pair is free. (Turkish)

My father said that I should use green, but I don't like green, so I decided to use blue. (Portuguese)

All of us were dancing while my father sang my favourite song. (Arabic - Meghreb)

positives: If I need a camera, I will use my mobile phone.
My father said that I should use green, but I don't like green, so I decided to use blue.
negatives: I'll do it if and when.

can_do_statement: Can use 'whatever', 'wherever', 'however', etc. as a subordinating conjunction, at the beginning of a sentence, to give focus.
example_raw:
Whatever you choose, you'll probably have to share it with other people. (Swedish)

Whatever the cause of the fall in the standard of your services is, we would strongly recommend that you take all the necessary measures to make sure that this won't happen again. (Romania; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2003; Romanian; Fail)

Wherever you go, you find shops, hotels and pubs which are full of tourists. (Greece; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2003; Greek; Pass)

Whoever we appoint, he/she should be a well-qualified, educated and flexible person. (Poland; C1 EFFECTIVE OPERATIONAL PROFICIENCY; 2001; Polish; Fail)

positives: Whatever you choose, you'll probably have to share it with other people.
Wherever you go, you find shops.

can_do_statement: Can use 'in that' as a subordinating conjunction, to give greater in-depth explanation, often in formal contexts.
example_raw:
Nowadays it is widely argued that professional sports are damaging to people's health in that they involve gruelling training sessions as an integral part of the occupation. (Russian)

It's often said that nowadays people must be proud of medical advances, in that life is getting considerably longer. (Spain; C2 MASTERY; 1993; Catalan; Fail)

positives: Nowadays it is widely argued that professional sports are damaging to people's health in that they involve gruelling training sessions.
It's often said that nowadays people must be proud of medical advances, in that life is getting considerably longer.

can_do_statement: Can use articles 'the', 'a' and 'an' before nouns. ► noun phrases
example_raw:
She lives in a small flat in the town - it's great! (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; German; Pass)

I have an appointment with my G.P. at 5.45 pm. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; Turkish; Pass)

positives: She lives in a flat.
I have an appointment.
negatives: It is a very good place.

can_do_statement: Can use 'a' + 'very' + adjectives in basic noun phrases. ► adverbs ►  noun phrases
example_raw:
He's a very good man. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; Mandarin; Pass)

It is a very beautiful place. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Russian; Pass)

It's a very nice town. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Slovak; Pass)

positives: He's a very good man.
It is a very beautiful place.

can_do_statement: Can use 'a' and 'an' before adjectives in a noun phrase. ► adjectives ►  noun phrases
example_raw:
You can make a quick snack, for example a sandwich. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2006; German; Pass)

We have a big garden and a small swimming pool. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Arabic - Other; Pass)

I like it because it is an interesting place. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Romanian; Fail)

It's an old house, about 50 years old. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2007; Arabic - Other; Fail)

positives: You can make a quick snack.
It is an interesting place.

can_do_statement: Can use 'the' in prepositional phrases relating to time.
example_raw:
I work at the weekend and I'm very busy from Monday to Friday. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2008; Polish; Pass)

I can come to see you on Friday in the morning. (A1 BREAKTHROUGH; 2009; Thai; Pass)

positives: I work at the weekend and I'm very busy.
I can come to see you on Friday in the morning.
negatives: I saw it on the table.
